title: Building a navigable dashboard in Excel

videos.script: A workbook full of pivot tables can answer almost any question. That is its problem. The owner of Café Serra has one question each month, and five minutes to answer it. {{question}} Is the business ahead of last year? And if it is not, where is it falling behind? This lesson builds one screen that answers that. {{screen}} Four numbers across the top. Revenue, bags, sales and the average sale. Each one sits beside the same months of last year. Below them, a chart of the months, because a total hides when things changed. Then the channels and the products, because that is where the owner can act. {{layout}} Nothing on that screen is new. The pivot tables come from lesson 10, the slicers from lesson 11, the charts from lesson 12, and the measures from lesson 16. What is new is the wiring. One slicer and one timeline, connected to every pivot table, so the whole screen moves together. {{wiring}} Then come the parts that make it usable by somebody else. A contents sheet with links. Headers that stay put. A sheet that a stray click cannot break. {{navigation}} And last, handing it over. A dashboard is only as fresh as its last refresh. And it carries every row of the data with it, wherever it is sent. You will check both before it leaves your computer. {{sharing}}
